column11: Why does FNH retain hepatobiliary contrast while its central scar does not?
column12: FNH is a hamartomatous focus of disorganized but functioning liver tissue containing hepatocytes and biliary ductules. The hepatocytes take up hepatobiliary agents, so the lesion is iso- to hyperintense on the hepatobiliary phase. The central scar is composed of biliary ductules and venules rather than normal hepatocyte-rich parenchyma, so the scar does not retain gadoxetate. Radiologic pivot: lesion retention with scar nonretention strongly supports FNH over adenoma.

column11: Why does a cavernous hemangioma show peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in?
column12: A cavernous hemangioma is composed of disorganized endothelial-lined vascular spaces supplied from the periphery. Contrast first opacifies peripheral vascular lakes, producing discontinuous nodules that match the blood pool, then progressively fills more central vascular spaces on later phases. Giant lesions may have a central nonenhancing degenerative/fibrotic region. Radiologic pivot: blood-pool-matching peripheral nodules with delayed centripetal fill-in are virtually pathognomonic in the right setting.

column11: Why can Budd-Chiari syndrome produce multiple hypervascular regenerative nodules that mimic HCC?
column12: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes chronic perfusion stress and parenchymal remodeling. Chronic disease produces peripheral hepatic atrophy with compensatory caudate hypertrophy and prominent regenerative nodules. These nodules contain functioning hepatocytes and can become hypervascular; hepatobiliary-agent retention therefore supports regenerative tissue rather than a nonhepatocellular metastasis. Radiologic pivot: interpret the nodules together with the global venous-outflow morphology and hepatobiliary retention rather than calling multifocal HCC from arterial hyperenhancement alone.

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core Radiology liver-mass sections were cross-checked against the fused RadPrimer/STATdx package.
🗂️ Summary
  • Start with the central/eccentric low-signal or low-density region: decide whether it is a true scar versus necrosis, hemorrhage, fat, fibrosis, or treated tumor.
  • Scar calcification strongly raises fibrolamellar HCC or giant hemangioma; calcification is uncommon in FNH, conventional HCC, adenoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and most metastases, although mucinous metastases can calcify.
  • Multiplicity is a major separator: FNH and cholangiocarcinoma are usually solitary; fibrolamellar HCC is almost always solitary; hemangioma, metastases, EHE, conventional HCC, and regenerative nodules may be multiple.
🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • FNH: bright homogeneous arterial enhancement; later isoattenuation/isointensity; T2-bright central scar with delayed enhancement using extracellular agents; lesion retains hepatobiliary contrast, while the scar does not.
  • Hemangioma: peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching blood pool with progressive centripetal fill-in; very bright T2 signal; giant lesions may have a nonenhancing fibrotic/cystic central region that can calcify.
  • Conventional HCC: arterial hyperenhancement with washout; large lesions may be heterogeneous or mosaic with necrosis; tumor-in-vein strongly supports HCC.
  • Hepatic adenoma: arterial hyperenhancement with later iso/hypoenhancement; heterogeneity can reflect fat or hemorrhage; out-of-phase signal loss supports intracellular lipid; low-density central areas may be necrosis/fibrosis rather than true scar.
  • Metastases: usually hypovascular and best seen on portal venous phase; central low density usually represents necrosis/fibrosis; mucinous metastases may calcify.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC: large heterogeneous mass in a young patient without cirrhosis, with a classic fibrotic central scar that is T1/T2 hypointense; calcification of the scar is a major clue.
  • Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma: large lobulated mass with delayed/progressive enhancement from fibrous stroma; supporting clues include peripheral biliary dilation, capsular retraction, volume loss, and vascular/biliary obstruction.
  • Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma: multiple peripheral/subcapsular lesions that may coalesce, often with target/halo appearance and capsular retraction; lesions are typically T1 low and T2 high.
  • Large regenerative nodules / NRH in Budd-Chiari: often multiple hypervascular nodules, some with central scars; hepatobiliary-agent retention supports functioning hepatocytes; chronic Budd-Chiari morphology provides the key context.
⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Common: focal nodular hyperplasia; hepatic cavernous hemangioma.
  • Less common: conventional HCC, hepatic adenoma, hepatic metastases, fibrolamellar HCC, intrahepatic/peripheral cholangiocarcinoma, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
  • Rare but important: large regenerative nodules / nodular regenerative hyperplasia, especially with Budd-Chiari syndrome.
⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • A central low-density or low-signal area is not automatically a scar: adenoma and metastases commonly create pseudo-scar appearances from hemorrhage, necrosis, fat, or fibrosis.
  • FNH central scar is T2 hyperintense and enhances late with extracellular contrast; fibrolamellar scar is fibrotic and T2 hypointense.
  • Portal-vein tumor invasion supports conventional HCC; capsular retraction plus biliary/portal obstruction supports cholangiocarcinoma.
  • In Budd-Chiari, multiple regenerative nodules can mimic HCC; assess the global venous-outflow morphology and hepatobiliary retention behavior.
⭐ Super Summary
  • For a liver mass with a central or eccentric scar-like region, solve the case by integrating scar composition/calcification, dynamic enhancement, T2 behavior, multiplicity, hepatobiliary contrast behavior, and secondary invasive/obstructive findings.

column15: For large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari syndrome, what hepatobiliary MRI behavior supports benign regenerative tissue?
column16:
Persistent uptake/retention of gadobenate dimeglumine in the nodules indicates functioning hepatocytes; deficient biliary ducts help explain retention within the lesions.
Recognition pivot: Hepatobiliary retention supports regenerative hepatocellular tissue rather than metastases.

column15: For large regenerative nodules / NRH in Budd-Chiari, what multiplicity and size pattern should be recognized?
column16:
Multiacinar large regenerative nodules are usually multiple and less than 4 cm and may have central scars.
Exam pivot: Numerous small-to-moderate scar-containing nodules in a Budd-Chiari liver should raise regenerative nodules before assuming multifocal malignancy.
